text.en: Nature changes slowly over the year: it warms, gets hot, rains and cools. Does it happen again next year? Yes, a natural rhythm repeats.

The repeating pattern in nature is what we call seasons. Name the seasons in your own region.
India has six seasons based on how nature changes every few months: Vasanta (spring), Grishma (summer), Varsha (monsoon), Sharad (autumn), Hemant (pre-winter) and Shishir (winter). Fill in the months for your region.
Winter in Kerala differs from winter in the Kashmir valley, and monsoon in Assam differs from Rajasthan. India has both Mawsynram, the wettest place on Earth, and the Thar Desert, one of the driest.
Farmers grow different crops in different seasons: some grow best in winter, some in summer heat, and some in the rains, which need more water.
Many songs are linked to seasons, and many festivals too: Pongal and Makar Sankranti are linked with winter harvest, Holi with spring when flowers bloom, Diwali with autumn after harvest, and Baisakhi, Gudi Padwa, Vishu and Rongali Bihu with the new year and harvest.
Seasons are not just changes in weather. They shape what plants grow, how animals live, and what people eat, wear and do. They remind us that change is natural and necessary.
In Odisha, when the koel sings, farmers know the rains are coming and begin planting.
During the monsoon, snakes come out of flooded burrows, which is why Nag Panchami is celebrated to show respect to nature.
When ants carry eggs to higher ground it is a natural sign that rain is coming soon.
Discuss: would you prefer one season all year?

problem.en: Match: Holi, Diwali, Pongal to seasons.

text.en: Holi is in spring when flowers bloom.
Diwali is in autumn after harvest.
Pongal is a winter harvest festival.

prompt.en: Why do seasons matter in our lives?

requiredIdeas.en: A pattern that repeats each year
Crops, food, clothes and festivals follow seasons

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking seasons are the same everywhere

points.en: A repeating pattern of change is a season.
